language: A program is a sequence of commands that change named, mutable state.
A program is the composition of pure functions over immutable values.
Objects bundle state with the methods that change it and send messages to each other.
A program is a set of facts and rules, and a search engine derives the answers.
The programmer states relations between variables and a solver finds the values.
Independent actors own their state and talk only through asynchronous messages.
Operations run when their inputs arrive, so the graph of data sets the order.
Values that change over time are first-class and the runtime propagates each change.
Adjacent program fragments compose functions, usually over a shared data stack.
The compiler checks one owner per value and releases the value when its owner leaves scope.
Programs declare effect operations, and handlers define how those operations execute and resume.
hardware: Simple fixed-length instructions overlap in a five-stage pipeline.
Hardware finds independent instructions at run time and issues several in each cycle.
The compiler packs independent operations into one long instruction at build time.
One instruction operates on a whole vector of data elements.
Thousands of threads run in lockstep groups and hide memory latency by switching groups.
Several cores share one coherent address space through caches.
Many cheap servers connected by a network act as one computer.
Hardware built for one class of work, such as the systolic arrays of a TPU.
Configurable logic blocks and interconnect form circuits rather than execute a fixed instruction stream.
Artificial neurons exchange sparse events, with memory and computation close together.
Dedicated secure silicon provides a trust anchor for boot verification and device attestation.
A parameterized program composes hardware components and emits a circuit description for a selected configuration.
os: All operating system services run in one privileged address space.
The kernel keeps only address spaces, threads and IPC; services run as user processes.
The kernel only multiplexes hardware safely and libraries implement the abstractions.
One application and the library OS that it needs compile into one single-address-space image.
A thin layer runs several complete operating systems on virtual hardware.
A process can use a resource only through an unforgeable capability that names it.
The scheduler guarantees that each task meets its deadline.
Networked machines provide system resources through common interfaces and a unified resource view.
Independent kernels on each core coordinate through explicit messages and replicate state rather than share it.
Separate monitors manage processor, memory and storage components across a network instead of one complete server.
The kernel isolates applications through fixed resource partitions and explicit controls on information flow.
The OS extends memory addresses to persistent storage, so applications use memory objects instead of separate file operations.
software: Clients send requests to a central server that owns the data.
Equal peers share resources directly without a central server.
Components publish events and other components react to them.
Each filter transforms a stream and passes it to the next filter.
Small services that each own their data talk over the network.
The platform runs a function for each request and bills only that run.
The primary copy of the data lives on the device and syncs to others when it can.
The state is the result of replaying an append-only log of events.
Separate models handle commands that change data and queries that read data.
The database engine executes inside the application process and accesses files without a separate server.
Packages are immutable values with explicit dependencies, so new versions coexist without changes to old versions.
External configuration supplies component dependencies, so each component can use an interface without a fixed implementation.
A server stores native data structures and exposes commands that operate on their contents directly.
Replicas accept independent updates and merge concurrent changes into the same state without a central coordinator.
